citation: Divett, T., Ingham, M., Richardson, G., Sigley, M., Rodger, C.J. (2023) Modeling Pipe to Soil Potentials From Geomagnetic Storms in Gas Pipelines in New Zealand. Space Weather. doi:10.1029/2023SW003601

dedupe_keys.name: pipe to soil potential model for geomagnetic storms in new zealand gas pipelines

description: This model estimates the pipe-to-soil potentials that geomagnetic storms induce in the gas transmission pipelines of New Zealand's North Island, to judge whether space weather is a corrosion hazard. Tim Divett, Malcolm Ingham, Gemma Richardson, Mark Sigley and Craig Rodger published it in the journal Space Weather in 2023. Operators keep pipe-to-soil potentials between -0.85 and -1.2 volts with cathodic protection; storm-induced geoelectric fields can push them outside that range. The authors represent the network as transmission lines and solve a nodal admittance matrix for potentials at nodes up to 5 km apart, then apply an idealised 100 mV/km field to the north and east. Potentials peak at pipeline ends in the direction of the field, follow the theoretical curve with deviations at branch lines and bends, and are sensitive to branch line coating conductance, which identifies the network locations most at risk of disbondment and corrosion. Coverage: the North Island gas pipeline network. Access: open-access article; no public code was found. Licence and cost: the article is CC BY 4.0 and free. Caveats: an idealised uniform field, not modelled storms, and coating parameters are estimates. It supports hazard exposure analysis of pipelines to space weather, and relates to the GeoNet geomagnetic data and the NOAA SWPC geoelectric field maps and products in the catalogue.
